claim: Insulin gene mutations are a leading cause of neonatal diabetes.
source: Insulin gene mutations are a leading cause of neonatal diabetes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about the etiology of neonatal diabetes.

claim: Insulin gene mutations can lead to proinsulin misfolding and its retention in endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: They can lead to proinsulin misfolding and its retention in endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known consequence of insulin gene mutations.

claim: Proinsulin misfolding results in increased ER-stress suggested to trigger beta-cell apoptosis.
source: This results in increased ER-stress suggested to trigger beta-cell apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a suggested mechanism, indicating it is based on prior literature.

claim: The mechanisms underlying beta-cell failure in humans remain unclear.
source: In humans, the mechanisms underlying beta-cell failure remain unclear.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap.

claim: Misfolded proinsulin impairs developing beta-cell proliferation without increasing apoptosis.
source: Here we show that misfolded proinsulin impairs developing beta-cell proliferation without increasing apoptosis.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) were generated from people carrying insulin (INS) mutations.

source: We generated induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from people carrying insulin (INS) mutations, engineered isogenic CRISPR-Cas9 mutation-corrected lines and differentiated them to beta-like cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: iPSCs were differentiated to beta-like cells.
source: We generated induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from people carrying insulin (INS) mutations, engineered isogenic CRISPR-Cas9 mutation-corrected lines and differentiated them to beta-like cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis showed increased ER-stress in INS-mutant beta-like cells compared with corrected controls.
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis showed increased ER-stress and reduced proliferation in INS-mutant beta-like cells compared with corrected controls.
evidence: This is a key finding from the scRNA-seq analysis presented in the study.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis showed reduced proliferation in INS-mutant beta-like cells compared with corrected controls.
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis showed increased ER-stress and reduced proliferation in INS-mutant beta-like cells compared with corrected controls.
evidence: This is a key finding from the scRNA-seq analysis presented in the study.

claim: Upon transplantation into mice, INS-mutant grafts presented reduced insulin secretion.
source: Upon transplantation into mice, INS-mutant grafts presented reduced insulin secretion and aggravated ER-stress.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo transplantation experiments.

claim: Upon transplantation into mice, INS-mutant grafts presented aggravated ER-stress.
source: Upon transplantation into mice, INS-mutant grafts presented reduced insulin secretion and aggravated ER-stress.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo transplantation experiments.

claim: Cell size was reduced in INS-mutant beta-like cells.
source: Cell size, mTORC1 signaling, and respiratory chain subunits expression were all reduced in INS-mutant beta-like cells, yet apoptosis was not increased at any stage.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of transplanted cells.

claim: mTORC1 signaling was reduced in INS-mutant beta-like cells.
source: Cell size, mTORC1 signaling, and respiratory chain subunits expression were all reduced in INS-mutant beta-like cells, yet apoptosis was not increased at any stage.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of transplanted cells.

claim: Respiratory chain subunits expression was reduced in INS-mutant beta-like cells.

source: Cell size, mTORC1 signaling, and respiratory chain subunits expression were all reduced in INS-mutant beta-like cells, yet apoptosis was not increased at any stage.

claim: Neonatal diabetes-associated INS-mutations lead to defective beta-cell mass expansion.
source: Our results demonstrate that neonatal diabetes-associated INS-mutations lead to defective beta-cell mass expansion, contributing to diabetes development.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: Defective beta-cell mass expansion contributes to diabetes development.
source: Our results demonstrate that neonatal diabetes-associated INS-mutations lead to defective beta-cell mass expansion, contributing to diabetes development.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: ER stress and unfolded protein response (UPR) are critical for the proper function and resilience of the beta-cell.
source: Among these, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and unfolded protein response (UPR) seem to be critical for the proper function and resilience of the beta-cell, and their role has been studied in different diabetes models (Brozzi and Eizirik, 2016; Cnop et al., 2017; Herbert and Laybutt, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: High quantities of insulin are transcribed, translated and ultimately secreted by beta-cells.
source: High quantities of insulin are transcribed, translated and ultimately secreted by beta-cells.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of beta-cell function.

claim: The UPR is highly efficient in beta-cells and adapts the ER loading and protein folding capacity to the insulin biosynthesis rate.
source: To cope with both the constant basal insulin secretion and the dynamic demand in response to elevated circulating glucose, the UPR is highly efficient in beta-cells, and adapts the ER loading and protein folding capacity to the insulin biosynthesis rate (Back and Kaufman, 2012; Vander Mierde et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: High levels of insulin biosynthesis generate a chronic sub-threshold ER-stress that suppresses beta-cell proliferation.
source: High levels of insulin biosynthesis generate a chronic sub-threshold ER-stress that suppresses beta-cell proliferation (Szabat et al., 2016), while induction of mild ER-stress in the context of hyperglycemia has been shown to induce beta-cell proliferation (Sharma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Induction of mild ER-stress in the context of hyperglycemia has been shown to induce beta-cell proliferation.
source: High levels of insulin biosynthesis generate a chronic sub-threshold ER-stress that suppresses beta-cell proliferation (Szabat et al., 2016), while induction of mild ER-stress in the context of hyperglycemia has been shown to induce beta-cell proliferation (Sharma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus (PNDM) is caused by mutations in genes controlling beta-cell development or functionality.
source: Permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus (PNDM) is caused by mutations in genes controlling beta-cell development or functionality, and is usually diagnosed before 6 months of age (Greeley et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PNDM is usually diagnosed before 6 months of age.
source: Permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus (PNDM) is caused by mutations in genes controlling beta-cell development or functionality, and is usually diagnosed before 6 months of age (Greeley et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Insulin gene mutations are among the most common causes for PNDM globally.
source: Insulin gene mutations are among the most common causes for PNDM globally (Huopio et al., 2016; Støy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Dominant negative heterozygous mutations that disrupt cysteine bridges within proinsulin lead to its misfolding, aggregation and accumulation in the ER.
source: Dominant negative heterozygous mutations that disrupt cysteine bridges within proinsulin lead to its misfolding, aggregation and accumulation in the ER (Herbach et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2010a; Park et al., 2010; Rajan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: High molecular weight proinsulin aggregates increase ER-stress and activate the UPR.
source: Accordingly, these high molecular weight proinsulin aggregates increase ER-stress and activate the UPR.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of proinsulin misfolding based on prior knowledge.

claim: Sustained UPR activation results in beta-cell dysfunction and the eventual onset of diabetes.
source: Sustained UPR activation results in beta-cell dysfunction and the eventual onset of diabetes (Colombo et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Akita mouse model of diabetes carries a proinsulin cysteine disruption mutation (C96Y).
source: This phenomenon has been studied extensively in the Akita mouse model of diabetes, which carries a proinsulin cysteine disruption mutation (C96Y) that leads to mutant proinsulin accumulation in the ER, enlarged ER, reduction of secretory granules and mitochondrial swelling (Izumi et al., 2003; Kayo and Koizumi, 1998; Wang et al., 1999; Yoshioka et al., 1997; Zuber et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Akita mouse model supported by citations.

claim: The Akita mouse C96Y mutation leads to mutant proinsulin accumulation in the ER, enlarged ER, reduction of secretory granules and mitochondrial swelling.
source: This phenomenon has been studied extensively in the Akita mouse model of diabetes, which carries a proinsulin cysteine disruption mutation (C96Y) that leads to mutant proinsulin accumulation in the ER, enlarged ER, reduction of secretory granules and mitochondrial swelling (Izumi et al., 2003; Kayo and Koizumi, 1998; Wang et al., 1999; Yoshioka et al., 1997; Zuber et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Akita mouse model supported by citations.

claim: The Munich mouse model carries Ins2 C95S mutation.
source: Similar findings have been reported from the Munich mouse model carrying Ins2 C95S mutation (Herbach et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Munich mouse model supported by a citation.

claim: Studies suggested that unresolved UPR resulted in beta-cell apoptosis via Chop (Ddit3) induction.
source: Although further studies suggested that unresolved UPR resulted in beta-cell apoptosis via Chop (Ddit3) induction (Oyadomari et al., 2002), significant differences in the number of apoptotic beta-cells were not observed in either model (Herbach et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: Significant differences in the number of apoptotic beta-cells were not observed in the Akita or Munich mouse models.
source: Although further studies suggested that unresolved UPR resulted in beta-cell apoptosis via Chop (Ddit3) induction (Oyadomari et al., 2002), significant differences in the number of apoptotic beta-cells were not observed in either model (Herbach et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior studies supported by a citation.

claim: Human induced pluripotent cell lines (iPSC) were derived from Finnish people carrying C96R and C109Y insulin mutations.
source: To study the role of proinsulin cysteine disrupting mutations in human beta-cells, we derived human induced pluripotent cell lines (iPSC) from Finnish people carrying C96R (the same cysteine as the Akita C96Y mutation) and C109Y insulin mutations (Huopio et al., 2016) and differentiated them in vitro to beta-like cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The C96R mutation affects the same cysteine as the Akita C96Y mutation.
source: To study the role of proinsulin cysteine disrupting mutations in human beta-cells, we derived human induced pluripotent cell lines (iPSC) from Finnish people carrying C96R (the same cysteine as the Akita C96Y mutation) and C109Y insulin mutations (Huopio et al., 2016) and differentiated them in vitro to beta-like cells.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the mutation studied.

claim: Isogenic correction of the cell lines using CRISPR-SpCas9 was employed to circumvent challenges associated with variable iPSC differentiation efficiency.
source: To circumvent the challenges associated with variable iPSC differentiation efficiency, we employed isogenic correction of the cell lines using CRISPR-SpCas9 (Balboa and Otonkoski, 2015; Hsu et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the rationale and approach used in the study.

source: Transplanted INS mutant beta-like cells exhibited lower insulin secretion and increased levels of ER-stress markers, together with reduced mTORC1 signaling and beta-cell size, without any apparent increase in apoptosis.

claim: Transplanted INS mutant beta-like cells exhibited increased levels of ER-stress markers.
source: Transplanted INS mutant beta-like cells exhibited lower insulin secretion and increased levels of ER-stress markers, together with reduced mTORC1 signaling and beta-cell size, without any apparent increase in apoptosis.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo transplantation experiments.

claim: Transplanted INS mutant beta-like cells exhibited reduced mTORC1 signaling.
source: Transplanted INS mutant beta-like cells exhibited lower insulin secretion and increased levels of ER-stress markers, together with reduced mTORC1 signaling and beta-cell size, without any apparent increase in apoptosis.

claim: Transplanted INS mutant beta-like cells exhibited reduced beta-cell size.

claim: PNDM-associated insulin mutations lead to inadequate development of a functional beta-cell mass.
source: Our findings suggest that PNDM-associated insulin mutations lead to inadequate development of a functional beta-cell mass.

claim: Two Finnish families with hereditary neonatal diabetes due to heterozygous insulin gene mutations were studied.
source: We studied two Finnish families with hereditary neonatal diabetes due to heterozygous insulin gene mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the patient cohort used in the study.

claim: Both missense mutations affect cysteine residues, resulting in the disruption of the proinsulin inter-chain disulphide bonds A7-B7 (mutation C96R) and A20-B19 (mutation C109Y).
source: Both missense mutations affect cysteine residues, resulting in the disruption of the proinsulin inter-chain disulphide bonds A7-B7 (mutation C96R) and A20-B19 (mutation C109Y) (Figure 1B) which are essential for the proper folding and biological activity of the insulin molecule (Chang et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the molecular consequences of the mutations studied, supported by a citation and Figure 1B.

claim: The disrupted disulphide bonds are essential for the proper folding and biological activity of the insulin molecule.
source: Both missense mutations affect cysteine residues, resulting in the disruption of the proinsulin inter-chain disulphide bonds A7-B7 (mutation C96R) and A20-B19 (mutation C109Y) (Figure 1B) which are essential for the proper folding and biological activity of the insulin molecule (Chang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Affected individuals of these families become hyperglycemic 3–4 months after birth.
source: Affected individuals of these families become hyperglycemic 3–4 months after birth.
evidence: This is a clinical observation from the patient cohort.

claim: Two affected newborns were monitored for the development of the disease.
source: Two affected newborns were monitored for the development of the disease.
evidence: This describes the clinical monitoring performed in the study.

claim: The affected newborns were born at normal gestational age, presenting normal birth weight and fasting plasma c-peptide levels.
source: They were born at normal gestational age, presenting normal birth weight and fasting plasma c-peptide levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a clinical observation from the patient cohort, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Continuous subcutaneous glucose monitoring demonstrated the gradual deterioration of glycemia during the first months of life.
source: Continuous subcutaneous glucose monitoring demonstrated the gradual deterioration of glycemia during the first months of life (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a clinical observation from the patient cohort, supported by Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Established iPSC expressed hallmark pluripotency markers.
source: They expressed hallmark pluripotency markers, presented normal karyotypes and were able to spontaneously differentiate to the three germ layers in embryoid bodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E).

claim: Established iPSC presented normal karyotypes.
source: They expressed hallmark pluripotency markers, presented normal karyotypes and were able to spontaneously differentiate to the three germ layers in embryoid bodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E).

claim: Sequencing of the insulin locus confirmed the presence in heterozygosis of the T to C change causing C96R mutation in iPSC line HEL71.4.
source: Sequencing of the insulin locus confirmed the presence in heterozygosis of the T to C change causing C96R mutation (iPSC line HEL71.4) (Figure 1C) and G to A change causing C109Y mutation (iPSC line HEL107.2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).

evidence: This is a characterization of the iPSC lines generated, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Differentiation protocols devised to obtain beta-cells from human pluripotent stem cells (PSC) are not equally efficient across cell lines.
source: Differentiation protocols devised to obtain beta-cells from human pluripotent stem cells (PSC) are not equally efficient across cell lines (Nostro et al., 2015; Sui et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

source: For disease modeling purposes, this variation in the differentiation from iPSC with different genetic backgrounds might obscure the phenotype caused by the mutation under study.

claim: Mutation-free isogenic iPSC lines were generated from the patient-derived HEL71.4 line by correcting the C96R mutation using CRISPR/SpCas9 genome editing.
source: Thus, we generated mutation-free isogenic iPSC lines from the patient-derived HEL71.4 line by correcting the C96R mutation using CRISPR/SpCas9 genome editing (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: A guide RNA (Ins8) cutting 9 base pairs away from the point mutation showed high cutting efficiency by T7 assay.
source: A guide RNA (Ins8) cutting 9 base pairs away from the point mutation showed high cutting efficiency by T7 assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–G).

claim: The recombination of the ssODN was efficient in HEK293 cells.
source: The recombination of the ssODN was efficient in HEK293 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–G).
evidence: This is a finding from the genome editing experiments, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–G.

claim: 27 iPSC colonies were recovered out of 384 sorted single cells (Cloning efficiency = 7.03%).
source: We recovered 27 iPSC colonies out of 384 sorted single cells (Cloning efficiency = 7.03%).

claim: 17 recombinant clones were found out of 22 screened (17/22 = 77% recombinant).
source: We screened the clones by PCR followed by BsrGI restriction and found 17 recombinant clones (17/22 = 77% recombinant) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).

claim: Clones F2, F10, G6 and A2 presented correction of the mutation with no chromosomal abnormalities.
source: Clones F2, F10, G6 and A2 presented correction of the mutation with no chromosomal abnormalities (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I).

claim: No mutations in putative off-targets were found in any clone.
source: No mutations in putative off-targets were found in any clone (Supplementary file 1 – Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the characterization of corrected clones.

claim: All INS mutant and INS corrected iPSC lines differentiated efficiently into definitive endoderm on day 3.
source: All INS mutant and INS corrected iPSC lines differentiated efficiently into definitive endoderm on day 3 (Figure 1D) and progressed to the pancreatic progenitor stage on day 12, presenting abundant PDX1+, NKX6.1+ and SOX9+ cells, with few NEUROG3+ and endocrine CHGA+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the differentiation experiments, supported by Figure 1D.

claim: iPSC lines progressed to the pancreatic progenitor stage on day 12, presenting abundant PDX1+, NKX6.1+ and SOX9+ cells, with few NEUROG3+ and endocrine CHGA+ cells.
source: All INS mutant and INS corrected iPSC lines differentiated efficiently into definitive endoderm on day 3 (Figure 1D) and progressed to the pancreatic progenitor stage on day 12, presenting abundant PDX1+, NKX6.1+ and SOX9+ cells, with few NEUROG3+ and endocrine CHGA+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the differentiation experiments, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: After 30 days of differentiation (final Stage 7, S7), differentiations from INS mutant and INS corrected iPSC yielded S7 aggregates that were composed of cells expressing PDX1 (an average across all iPSC lines of 73 ± 12% SD PDX1+ cells, n = 10).
source: After 30 days of differentiation (final Stage 7, S7), we characterized the islet-like aggregates by cytometry. Differentiations from INS mutant and INS corrected iPSC yielded S7 aggregates that were composed of cells expressing PDX1 (an average across all iPSC lines of 73 ± 12% SD PDX1+ cells, n = 10) and NKX6.1 (an average across all iPSC lines of 37 ± 15% SD, NKX6.1+, n = 23) (Figure 1E) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the differentiation experiments, supported by Figure 1E.

claim: After 30 days of differentiation (final Stage 7, S7), differentiations from INS mutant and INS corrected iPSC yielded S7 aggregates that were composed of cells expressing NKX6.1 (an average across all iPSC lines of 37 ± 15% SD, NKX6.1+, n = 23).
source: After 30 days of differentiation (final Stage 7, S7), we characterized the islet-like aggregates by cytometry. source: On average across all iPSC lines, 41% (±14% SD, n = 25) of the S7 cells were INS+, with 18% (±6% SD, n = 23) of the cells expressing both INS and NKX6.1, a sign of bona fide beta-cells (Nostro et al., 2015) (Results pooled by genotype presented in Figure 1E–F, results of individual iPSC lines presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).

claim: On average across all iPSC lines, 18% (±6% SD, n = 23) of the S7 cells expressed both INS and NKX6.1, a sign of bona fide beta-cells.
source: On average across all iPSC lines, 41% (±14% SD, n = 25) of the S7 cells were INS+, with 18% (±6% SD, n = 23) of the cells expressing both INS and NKX6.1, a sign of bona fide beta-cells (Nostro et al., 2015) (Results pooled by genotype presented in Figure 1E–F, results of individual iPSC lines presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the differentiation experiments, with the interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: The number of INS+ cells at S7 was significantly different between INS mutant (31 ± 10% SD; n = 9) and corrected cells (49 ± 13% SD; n = 16).
source: The number of INS+ cells at S7 was significantly different between INS mutant (31 ± 10% SD; n = 9) and corrected cells (49 ± 13% SD; n = 16) (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the differentiation experiments, supported by Figure 1E.

claim: A total of 2,287 single cells from INS C96R and INS corrected Stage 7 islet-like aggregates were sequenced with a mean depth of 38,329 aligned reads/cell.
source: A total of 2 287 single cells from INS C96R and INS corrected Stage 7 islet-like aggregates were sequenced with a mean depth of 38 329 aligned reads/cell.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the scRNA-seq experiment.

claim: Out of 2,287 sequenced cells, 2,171 (94.9%) passed quality control.
source: Out of these cells, 2 171 (94.9%) passed quality control.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the scRNA-seq data processing.

claim: An average of 3,321 unique transcripts (UMI) and 1,391 genes were detected per cell.
source: An average of 3 321 unique transcripts (UMI) and 1391 genes were detected per cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1 – Table 9, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the scRNA-seq analysis, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Clustering analysis of all cells from both genotypes distinguished four different cell populations: beta-like cells, endocrine progenitor cells, alpha cells, and proliferating alpha cells.
source: Clustering analysis of all cells from both genotypes distinguished four different cell populations, expressing markers of beta-cells (beta-like cells), endocrine progenitor cells (progenitor cells), alpha cells (alpha-like cells), and proliferating alpha cells (proliferating alpha-like cells) (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–B) (Supplementary file 1 – Table 2) (Segerstolpe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq clustering analysis, supported by Figure 2A–B.

claim: The highest levels of INS expression were observed in the beta-like cluster.
source: The highest levels of INS expression were observed in the beta-like cluster (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis, supported by Figure 2B–C.

claim: A resampling procedure confirmed the robustness of the clustering results.
source: A resampling procedure confirmed the robustness of the clustering results (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C–D).
evidence: This is a validation of the clustering analysis, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4C–D.

claim: Mutant beta-like cells presented significant upregulation of chaperone genes HSPA5, HSPA8 and HSP90B1.

claim: Mutant beta-like cells presented significant upregulation of components of the ER associated degradation (ERAD) pathway HM13, HERPUD1, SEC61B and SDF2L1.

claim: SDF2L1 has been shown to interact with misfolded proinsulin and mediate its degradation.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Expression of the CDKN1C gene was increased in mutant beta-like cells.
source: Expression of the CDKN1C gene was also increased. The gene product, p57/Kip2, is an important inhibitor of human beta-cell proliferation (Avrahami et al., 2014), suggesting reduced proliferation of the INS C96R cells.

claim: The gene product of CDKN1C, p57/Kip2, is an important inhibitor of human beta-cell proliferation.
source: Expression of the CDKN1C gene was also increased. The gene product, p57/Kip2, is an important inhibitor of human beta-cell proliferation (Avrahami et al., 2014), suggesting reduced proliferation of the INS C96R cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The INS gene was upregulated in INS C96R cells, together with other insulin secretion related genes (CPE, SCGN, DLK1).
